script: Bread rises because yeast produces carbon dioxide, but the gas alone would escape without the second half of the process. As flour is mixed with water, two proteins in the flour link together into an elastic network called gluten. Kneading aligns those links, and the network becomes able to stretch without tearing. The carbon dioxide released by the yeast collects in small pockets already present in the dough, and the gluten network holds the walls of those pockets in place while they expand. This is why a dough that has not been kneaded enough produces a dense loaf even when the yeast is perfectly healthy: the gas is made and lost. Temperature governs the timing of both halves. Yeast works faster as it warms, up to about thirty-five degrees, while the gluten network becomes weaker as it warms. A dough left somewhere very warm therefore produces gas faster than the structure can hold it, and collapses. The long, cool rises favoured by bakers are a way of keeping the two processes in step, and the flavour that develops during them is a side effect rather than the reason.

items.stem: What holds the gas inside the dough?
items.rationale: The gluten network holds the walls of the gas pockets in place while they expand.

items.stem: Why does under-kneaded dough give a dense loaf?
items.rationale: The passage says the gas is made and lost when the network has not been developed by kneading.

items.stem: What does warmth do to the two processes?
options: Speeds one and weakens the other
items.rationale: Yeast works faster as it warms while the gluten network becomes weaker.

items.stem: Why can a very warm dough collapse?
items.rationale: Gas is produced faster than the weakened structure can hold, so the dough collapses.

items.stem: How does the writer describe the flavour of a long rise?
options: A side effect of the timing
The main aim of the method
items.rationale: The final sentence calls the flavour a side effect rather than the reason for the long cool rise.

script: A suspension bridge carries its load in a way that is almost the opposite of a beam. In a beam, the material above the middle is squeezed and the material below is stretched, and the beam can only span as far as its own weight allows before the stretching becomes too much. A suspension bridge removes that limit by putting the whole span in tension. The deck hangs from vertical cables, those cables hang from two main cables, and the main cables run over the towers and down into anchorages buried in rock or concrete at each end. Every part of that chain is being pulled, not bent, and steel in tension is far stronger than steel in bending. The towers do the one job that is not tension: they are compressed, pushed downwards by the main cables passing over them. This is why the towers of a suspension bridge are so much thicker than they appear necessary for their height. The anchorages matter just as much and are almost invisible, because they resist the horizontal pull of the cables. A suspension bridge that lost an anchorage would not sag; the whole span would move.

items.stem: What limits how far a beam can span?
items.rationale: A beam can only span as far as its own weight allows before the stretching becomes too much.

items.stem: How does a suspension bridge avoid that limit?
options: It puts the span in tension
items.rationale: The bridge removes the limit by putting the whole span in tension rather than bending.

items.stem: What force acts on the towers?
items.rationale: The towers are compressed, pushed downwards by the main cables passing over them.

items.stem: Why are the towers thicker than expected?
items.rationale: Their thickness follows from the compression the main cables put on them.

items.stem: What do the anchorages resist?
items.rationale: The anchorages resist the horizontal pull of the cables, which is why losing one would move the whole span.

script: Noise-cancelling headphones work by producing a sound that cancels another sound. A microphone on the outside of the earcup records what is arriving, a processor inverts that signal, and a speaker plays the inverted version into the ear at the same moment. Two waves that are exact opposites sum to nothing, and the listener hears silence where the noise would have been. The method works far better on some sounds than on others, and the reason is timing. Low, steady sounds such as an aircraft engine change slowly, so the processor has time to measure the wave and produce its opposite before the wave has moved on. A voice, or a door closing, changes far faster than the system can follow, and by the time the opposite is played the original has already passed. This is why passengers report that cancellation removes the engine and leaves the conversation two rows back. Most headphones therefore combine the electronic method with a physical one, sealing the ear against high frequencies that the processor cannot catch, and much of what people attribute to cancellation is in fact the seal.

items.stem: What does the processor do?
items.rationale: The processor inverts the signal captured by the external microphone.

items.stem: Why do low steady sounds cancel well?
options: They are quieter to begin with
items.rationale: They change slowly, so the processor has time to produce the opposite wave before the sound moves on.

items.stem: Why does speech survive cancellation?
options: It changes too fast to follow
It is louder than an engine
It comes from behind the wearer
It is picked up by the seal
items.rationale: A voice changes faster than the system can follow, so the opposite arrives too late.

items.stem: What does the physical seal do?
items.rationale: The seal blocks high frequencies the processor cannot catch.

items.stem: What point does the writer make about the seal?
options: It does much of the work
items.rationale: Much of what people attribute to cancellation is in fact the seal.

script: A vaccine works by presenting the immune system with something that looks like a pathogen but cannot cause the disease. The immune system responds as it would to an infection, and part of that response is the production of memory cells that persist long after the response has ended. When the real pathogen arrives, those memory cells recognise it and the response begins in hours rather than days, which is usually the difference between an infection that is stopped and one that takes hold. What is presented varies. Some vaccines use a weakened form of the pathogen, some use a killed form, and some use only a single protein from its surface. The newest use a set of instructions that the body's own cells read in order to make that protein themselves, after which the instructions are destroyed. In every case the target is the same: a shape on the outside of the pathogen that the immune system can learn. This is why a pathogen that changes that shape frequently, such as influenza, requires a new vaccine each year, while one that changes it slowly can be covered by a vaccine given once.

items.stem: What makes the second response faster?
options: The pathogen is weaker the second time
items.rationale: Memory cells persist and recognise the pathogen, so the response begins in hours rather than days.

items.stem: What do the newest vaccines supply?
options: A killed form of the pathogen
items.rationale: They supply instructions the body's own cells read to make the protein, after which the instructions are destroyed.

items.stem: What is the target in every case?
options: A shape on the pathogen's surface
items.rationale: The target is a shape on the outside of the pathogen that the immune system can learn.

items.stem: Why does influenza need a yearly vaccine?
items.rationale: A pathogen that changes that shape frequently requires a new vaccine each year.

items.stem: What is true of a slowly changing pathogen?
items.rationale: One that changes its surface slowly can be covered by a vaccine given once.

script: The reason a city is several degrees warmer than the countryside around it is usually given as the heat released by traffic and buildings, and that contribution is real but small. The larger part of the effect is geometric and has nothing to do with energy use at all. A rural surface loses heat at night by radiating it to the sky, and the sky is a very cold sink. A street in a city cannot see much of the sky. Its surfaces radiate towards the buildings opposite, which radiate back, so the heat absorbed during the day leaves far more slowly. The narrower the street relative to the height of the buildings, the smaller the visible patch of sky and the slower the loss, and measurements of this ratio predict night-time temperature differences across a city better than any measure of population or traffic. Two other properties compound it. Stone, brick and asphalt store more heat than soil and vegetation, so more is available to release; and a city has far less water. A leaf spends the day evaporating water, and evaporation removes heat without raising temperature at all, which is why a park inside a city can be several degrees cooler than the street beside it while receiving the same sunlight. The practical consequence is that the strongest interventions are not the ones aimed at the heat produced. Widening a street is not usually possible, but planting it changes both the water and, over time, the sunlight that reaches the stone.

items.stem: What is the largest cause of urban warmth?
options: The restricted view of the sky
items.rationale: The passage says the larger part of the effect is geometric: city surfaces cannot radiate to much of the sky.

items.stem: What does the street-to-building ratio predict?
items.rationale: Measurements of that ratio predict night-time temperature differences better than population or traffic.

items.stem: Why do urban materials add to the effect?
options: They store more heat than soil
items.rationale: Stone, brick and asphalt store more heat than soil and vegetation, so more is available to release.

items.stem: How does evaporation cool a park?
options: It removes heat without warming air
items.rationale: Evaporation removes heat without raising temperature at all.

items.stem: What follows for practical intervention?
options: Little can be done at all
items.rationale: The strongest interventions are not aimed at heat produced; planting changes the water and the sunlight reaching stone.

script: An electrical grid must match supply to demand continuously, and the mechanism that enforces this is the frequency of the alternating current itself. Across a synchronised grid, generators spin in step, and their combined rotating mass sets a common frequency, nominally fifty or sixty cycles a second. When demand exceeds supply, the extra load acts as a brake: the generators slow fractionally and the frequency falls. When supply exceeds demand the reverse happens. Nothing measures the imbalance directly. The frequency is the measurement, available everywhere on the grid at once and requiring no communication, which is why control systems built long before computers could work at all. The rotating mass matters for a second reason. It stores energy, and that stored energy is what keeps the frequency from moving too quickly while slower controls respond. A grid with many large spinning generators has a great deal of this inertia, and a sudden loss of one generator produces a slow, correctable dip. Solar panels and most wind turbines connect through power electronics and contribute no rotating mass, so a grid that has replaced spinning plant with them has less time to react to the same fault, even when it has ample capacity. This is a distinct problem from having enough generation, it is frequently confused with it, and the remedies are different: synthetic inertia from batteries responding in milliseconds, or spinning machines kept turning for no purpose but their mass. Two further points are worth separating from the first. Inertia is not a service anyone was ever paid for, because it was an unavoidable by-product of the machines that generated the electricity, and markets do not price what arrives free. And the response required is measured in fractions of a second, which is faster than any human decision and faster than most contracts are written to describe.

items.stem: What signals an imbalance on the grid?
items.rationale: Nothing measures the imbalance directly; the frequency is the measurement, available everywhere at once.

items.stem: What happens when demand exceeds supply?
items.rationale: The extra load acts as a brake, so generators slow fractionally and the frequency falls.

items.stem: What does rotating mass provide?
options: Time for slower controls to act
items.rationale: Stored energy in the rotating mass keeps frequency from moving too quickly while slower controls respond.

items.stem: Why do solar panels change the picture?
items.rationale: They connect through power electronics and contribute no rotating mass, reducing the grid's inertia.

items.stem: What confusion does the writer warn against?
items.rationale: The passage says the inertia problem is distinct from having enough generation and is frequently confused with it.

script: Antibiotic resistance is often described as bacteria learning to survive a drug, which gets the mechanism backwards. Bacteria do not adapt within a lifetime. In any large population a few individuals already carry a mutation, or a fragment of imported genetic material, that happens to blunt the drug. Before the drug is used those individuals are usually at a disadvantage, because the resistance machinery costs energy to run. The drug reverses that arithmetic. It removes the majority and leaves the few, which then multiply into the space the majority occupied. Nothing has learned anything; the population has been filtered. Two features of bacterial life make the filtering unusually fast. Generations are measured in minutes, so a rare variant becomes common in days rather than millennia. And bacteria exchange genetic material sideways, between individuals and even between species, so a resistance gene that arises in a harmless organism in a drain can end up in a dangerous one in a hospital without any ancestral link between them. This is why the standard advice about finishing a course matters, and why it is more subtle than it sounds. A course stopped early leaves behind the partially resistant, which are precisely the population the full course would have removed. But the same logic makes an unnecessary course harmful, because it applies the filter for no benefit, and the resistance it selects for does not stay in the person who took it. One further consequence is worth naming, since it is where the arithmetic reaches the individual. The resistance selected inside one person does not remain there. It travels in the ordinary way that bacteria travel, through hands and surfaces and food, so the cost of an unnecessary prescription is paid by a population and the benefit, when there is one, is paid to a patient.

items.stem: What is wrong with saying bacteria learn?
options: The population is filtered, not taught
items.rationale: Resistant individuals already exist; the drug removes the rest, so the population is filtered rather than taught.

items.stem: Why are resistant bacteria rare before the drug?
items.rationale: The resistance machinery costs energy to run, putting those individuals at a disadvantage beforehand.

items.stem: Why is the filtering fast?
items.rationale: Generations are measured in minutes, so a rare variant becomes common within days.

items.stem: What does sideways exchange allow?
items.rationale: Bacteria exchange genetic material between individuals and species, with no ancestral link required.

items.stem: Why is an unnecessary course harmful?
items.rationale: An unnecessary course applies the filter for no benefit, and the resistance selected does not stay with that person.

script: A weather forecast is not a prediction in the way a tide table is. The equations governing the atmosphere are known and are not in doubt, but they are sensitive to their starting conditions in a way that places a hard limit on how far ahead they can be run. Two states of the atmosphere that differ by less than any instrument can detect will, after about a week, have diverged into two entirely different weather patterns. This is not a failure of measurement that better instruments will fix; the divergence is a property of the equations. Forecasting therefore stopped trying to produce one answer some decades ago. A modern forecast runs the model many times from slightly different starting points, each within the range the observations allow, and reports what the resulting spread looks like. When the runs agree, the forecast is confident and usually right. When they scatter, the honest output is a probability, and the familiar percentage attached to rain is exactly that: the proportion of runs producing rain at that place and hour. Two consequences follow that the public presentation often obscures. A forecast can be well made and still wrong on the day, if the day turns out to be one of the minority outcomes; and a forecast that never says thirty per cent is not more confident but less informative, because it is hiding the spread rather than resolving it. A final point concerns how the spread is presented rather than produced. Broadcasters and applications generally show the mean of the runs, because a single number fits the space available, and the mean of a scattered set is the outcome the model considers least characteristic rather than most. The spread exists in the data of every forecast issued; what varies is whether anyone is shown it.

items.stem: Why is a forecast limited to about a week?
options: The equations are not fully known
items.rationale: Two states differing below detection diverge into different patterns after about a week, as a property of the equations.

items.stem: How does a modern forecast work?
options: It runs the model many times
It uses a single best estimate
items.rationale: The model is run many times from slightly different starting points within the observational range.

items.stem: What does a rain percentage represent?
options: The share of runs producing rain
The area likely to be wet
items.rationale: The percentage is the proportion of runs producing rain at that place and hour.

items.stem: When is a forecast confident?
items.rationale: Agreement among the runs is what makes a forecast confident and usually right.

items.stem: What does avoiding middling percentages do?
items.rationale: A forecast that never says thirty per cent is less informative because it hides the spread rather than resolving it.

script: The question of how a migrating bird finds its way has been answered several times, and each answer has turned out to be one component of a system rather than the mechanism. The sun was established first, and with it the requirement for a clock: using the sun for direction is useless unless the animal knows the time of day, and experiments that shifted birds' internal clocks by six hours shifted their headings by ninety degrees, which is what a clock-and-sun model predicts exactly. Star patterns came next, demonstrated in planetaria where the artificial sky could be rotated and the birds turned with it. Neither survives cloud, and birds fly through cloud, so a third component was sought and found in the magnetic field. Here the account becomes stranger. Birds do not appear to sense the field's polarity, which a compass needle does, but its inclination — the angle at which the field lines enter the ground — which distinguishes towards the pole from towards the equator without distinguishing north from south. The receptor is still argued over, with evidence for a chemical reaction in the eye that is sensitive to field orientation and requires light, which would make the magnetic sense something closer to vision than to touch. What has become clear is that the components are not redundant copies of one another. They are calibrated against each other, and a bird deprived of one for long enough recalibrates the others, which is why single-cue experiments produced answers that were each correct and each incomplete. The practical importance of that last point is easy to overlook. A bird carrying several calibrated systems is robust in a way a bird carrying one would not be, and the experimental history reflects the robustness rather than any perversity in the animal. Remove the stars and the magnetic sense takes over; remove the magnetic field and the sun and the stars suffice; and only by removing them in combination, which no natural night does, is the animal genuinely lost.

items.stem: Why does sun navigation require a clock?
options: The sun gives distance, not direction
items.rationale: Using the sun for direction is useless unless the animal knows the time of day.

items.stem: What did the six-hour clock shift produce?
items.rationale: Shifting the internal clock by six hours shifted headings by ninety degrees, as the model predicts.

items.stem: What do birds sense in the magnetic field?
options: The polarity, as a compass does
items.rationale: They appear to sense inclination rather than polarity, distinguishing poleward from equatorward.

items.stem: Why might the magnetic sense resemble vision?
options: It is located in the beak
It depends on the sun's angle
items.rationale: Evidence points to a light-dependent chemical reaction in the eye that is sensitive to field orientation.

items.stem: Why were single-cue experiments incomplete?
items.rationale: The components are calibrated against each other and a bird deprived of one recalibrates the others.

script: Concrete is the most used manufactured material on earth, and the chemistry that makes it useful is also the source of its principal environmental cost. Cement is produced by heating limestone with clay to about fourteen hundred and fifty degrees. Two separate emissions follow, and conflating them has confused a good deal of public discussion. The first is the fuel burned to reach that temperature, which can in principle be replaced by electricity or hydrogen. The second is chemical and cannot: limestone is calcium carbonate, and turning it into the calcium oxide that cement requires releases carbon dioxide as a matter of stoichiometry, regardless of how the heat is supplied. Roughly six tenths of the emissions from cement are of this second kind. There is a partial and slow reversal. Cured concrete absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, reforming carbonate at exposed surfaces, and over the life of a structure this recovers perhaps a fifth of what was released, more if the material is eventually crushed and exposed. The routes now being pursued follow from this arithmetic rather than from ambition. Replacing part of the cement with slag or ash reduces the amount of clinker needed; designing structures to use less concrete for the same load attacks the same term; and capturing the chemical carbon dioxide at the kiln, where it emerges in a concentrated stream rather than diluted in flue gas, is easier than capture almost anywhere else. What none of these does is eliminate the second emission, and any account that promises to has usually confused it with the first. A last observation belongs with the arithmetic rather than the ambition. Concrete is used in such quantity that a proportional saving of a few per cent outweighs the complete elimination of many smaller industries, and this is the reason the material attracts attention disproportionate to the difficulty of any single decision about it.

items.stem: What are the two emissions from cement?
options: Burning fuel and a chemical release
items.rationale: The first is the fuel burned to reach temperature; the second is the chemical release from converting limestone.

items.stem: Why can the second not be avoided by clean energy?
options: It follows from the reaction itself
items.rationale: Turning calcium carbonate into calcium oxide releases carbon dioxide as a matter of stoichiometry.

items.stem: What share is the chemical emission?
items.rationale: Roughly six tenths of cement emissions are of the chemical kind.

items.stem: What does cured concrete do over time?
items.rationale: Cured concrete absorbs carbon dioxide at exposed surfaces, recovering perhaps a fifth over a structure's life.

items.stem: Why is capture at the kiln comparatively easy?
items.rationale: The chemical carbon dioxide emerges in a concentrated stream rather than diluted in flue gas.

script: The persistence of a language in a bilingual community is often treated as a matter of attitude, and attitude turns out to explain less than the arithmetic of who talks to whom. A minority language survives when a child hears it from enough different speakers in enough different situations, and both parts of that sentence carry weight. A child who hears the language from two parents and nobody else acquires it, but acquires a version narrowed to domestic vocabulary, and abandons it at the point where school and friendship supply richer alternatives. The threshold is not a proportion of the population but a density of contact, which is why a language can survive in a village of four hundred and disappear in a city neighbourhood containing four thousand of its speakers scattered across it. Institutional support acts on the same variable rather than on attitude. A school that teaches in the language does not principally change how children feel about it; it manufactures situations in which the language is the only practical medium, and it puts children in contact with adults who are not their parents. This is also why broadcasting has generally disappointed those who invested in it. It supplies input without interaction, and the evidence from several revival programmes is that input alone raises comprehension without producing speakers. The uncomfortable implication is that the interventions that work are expensive and local, while the ones that are cheap and visible are the ones that do not. There is a further asymmetry that programmes tend to discover late. The children who most need the manufactured situations are those whose households already speak the majority language, and they are also the children least likely to be enrolled in a school that offers them, because enrolment is usually voluntary and is chosen by the parents whose own contact with the language is strongest.

items.stem: What matters more than attitude?
items.rationale: Survival depends on hearing the language from enough speakers in enough situations, a density of contact rather than a proportion.

items.stem: What happens to a child taught only by parents?
options: The language replaces the majority one
items.rationale: Such a child acquires a version narrowed to domestic vocabulary and abandons it when richer alternatives appear.

items.stem: Why can a village succeed where a city fails?
items.rationale: The threshold is density of contact, so a village of four hundred can succeed where scattered thousands do not.

items.stem: How does a school actually help?
options: It creates situations needing the language
items.rationale: A school manufactures situations in which the language is the only practical medium and adds non-parental adults.

items.stem: Why has broadcasting disappointed?
items.rationale: Broadcasting supplies input without interaction, which raises comprehension without producing speakers.

script: Why some materials conduct electricity and others do not is a question that classical physics answered wrongly for a generation, and the correct answer is worth following because it explains a third category that classical physics could not accommodate at all. In an isolated atom, electrons occupy discrete energy levels. Bring a great many atoms together into a solid and those levels smear into bands of permitted energies separated by gaps in which no electron may sit. Whether the material conducts depends entirely on where the electrons stop filling. If the highest occupied band is only partly full, an electron can move to a marginally higher energy within the same band, and a marginally higher energy is what an applied voltage offers; the material is a metal. If a band is exactly filled and the next is far above it, no such small step exists, the electrons cannot respond to ordinary voltages, and the material is an insulator. The third case is the interesting one. If the gap is small, then at room temperature a modest number of electrons are lifted across it by heat alone, leaving behind vacancies that themselves behave as mobile positive charges. Such a material conducts weakly, conducts better when warmed, and can have its conductivity altered by many orders of magnitude by adding a trace of a foreign element that donates or removes electrons. That last property is the whole basis of the semiconductor industry, and it is a direct consequence of the gap being small rather than absent, which is why the useful materials sit in a narrow window between the metals and the insulators. The window is narrow in a further sense that matters industrially. A gap too small leaves a material whose conductivity changes so steeply with temperature that a device made from it behaves differently on a cold morning, and a gap too large leaves one requiring impractical voltages, so the materials in use occupy a range of about one to three electron volts rather than being merely somewhere between the extremes.

items.stem: What happens to energy levels in a solid?
items.rationale: Bringing many atoms together smears discrete levels into bands separated by forbidden gaps.

items.stem: What makes a material a metal?
options: Its highest band is partly full
items.rationale: A partly full highest band lets an electron move to a marginally higher energy, which is what a voltage offers.

items.stem: Why does an insulator not conduct?
options: Its atoms are too far apart
items.rationale: A filled band with the next far above leaves no small step, so electrons cannot respond to ordinary voltages.

items.stem: What do the vacancies behave as?
items.rationale: Electrons lifted across a small gap leave vacancies that behave as mobile positive charges.

items.stem: What does adding a trace element achieve?
options: A reduction in the band gap
items.rationale: A trace element that donates or removes electrons alters conductivity by many orders of magnitude.
